title: [v0.5.4] Acceptance: verify portability and compatibility
author: mcpdev80
body:
## Goal

Close v0.5 by proving that the frozen BaseHarbor contracts are stable, portable and ready for later availability/topology semantics and new runtimes without changing portable application intent.

This release is an acceptance/hardening release, not a feature expansion.

> **Developer experience first.**
>
> **No new knob without a demonstrated need.**

## Portability questions

The architecture must be able to answer **yes** to all of these without implementing the future platform yet:

1. Can the same portable application contract be realized by Compose today and Kubernetes/OpenShift later?
2. Can a capability provider later move from a local/reference implementation to an AWS/Azure/GCP managed service without rewriting application intent?
3. Can runtime, capability provider, identity, networking, storage and artifact/distribution concerns remain independent?
4. Can future cloud support be added without a monolithic `aws`, `azure` or `gcp` application mode?
5. Can later availability/topology requirements be negotiated by runtimes/providers without hard-coding Kubernetes concepts into the application contract?

## Kubernetes contract-readiness acceptance

Before v0.5 closes, perform an explicit paper/design acceptance for a later namespace-restricted Kubernetes runtime.

The review must prove that the frozen contracts can express all required information **without adding Kubernetes concepts to portable application intent**.

The scenario must be representable as:

```text
portable application intent
        +
deployment/operator state:
  runtime target
  environment
  runtime access reference
  platform resource references
        ↓
restricted runtime provider
        ↓
plan / preflight / apply / observe / verify
```

The acceptance scenario must cover:

- pre-provisioned target scope;
- runtime credentials/access supplied outside portable intent;
- platform-owned shared infrastructure;
- BaseHarbor-owned application resources;
- a missing permission affecting one feature only;
- an unavailable cluster/platform fact causing `unverifiable` rather than false success;
- foreign ownership/conflict;
- no runtime-specific field added to the portable application contract.

This is an architecture acceptance only; no Kubernetes implementation belongs in v0.5.


## Target portability acceptance

Target semantics are inherited from **#408 / v0.4.15**. This issue does not define Target, Access or Scope.

It proves that the already-frozen Target contract remains portable across conforming runtimes:

- arbitrary existing platform scopes can be referenced without changing portable application intent;
- provider-specific Scope interpretation stays behind the Runtime Provider boundary;
- platform/external Scope ownership is preserved;
- destroy removes only BaseHarbor-owned resources and never an externally/platform-owned Scope;
- future Kubernetes/OpenShift realization requires no new Target semantics or Kubernetes fields in `baseharbor.yaml`.


## Capability substitution acceptance

The v0.5 portability acceptance must include at least one negative provider-substitution test.

Scenario:

- Application requires capability X plus semantic feature Y.
- Provider A implements X plus Y: supported.
- Provider B implements X but not Y: unsupported before mutation.

Use an existing BaseHarbor capability family and a demonstrated realistic requirement rather than inventing a speculative feature taxonomy.

This proves that provider portability means semantic compatibility, not merely sharing the same capability label.

## Acceptance

- [ ] The test does not rely on provider product names in portable application intent.

- [ ] A negative provider-substitution scenario proves semantic incompatibility is rejected before mutation.

- [ ] An arbitrary pre-existing target scope such as `r2-4b-dt-test` can be selected without changing portable application intent.
- [ ] Destroy never deletes a platform/external target scope itself; it removes only BaseHarbor-owned resources within it.

- [ ] `unsupported`, `unverifiable`, authorization denial, conflict and foreign ownership remain distinct machine-readable states.

- [ ] Missing permission/capability can block one feature without unnecessarily blocking unrelated lifecycle operations.

- [ ] Future runtime target, access source and platform-resource references require no portable-contract Kubernetes fields.

- [ ] A namespace-restricted Kubernetes thought experiment fits entirely within the frozen deployment/runtime boundaries. matrix

Exercise at least:

- fresh application -> init -> plan -> up -> status -> doctor;
- existing supported application contract;
- supported old BaseHarbor state migration;
- capability-provider protocol compatibility;
- full agent-native Compose lifecycle through MCP/JSON using shared BaseHarbor semantics;
- drift -> repair;
- backup -> restore -> real verification;
- update/upgrade -> verification/recovery;
- ownership-safe destroy;
- shared/application/external provider placement where supported;
- secret-safe diagnostics/evidence.

Compose remains the reference runtime for executable acceptance.

## Portability review

Perform a semantic inventory of all important public/state fields and classify them as:

- portable application intent;
- environment/operator policy;
- capability-provider state;
- runtime state;
- protected/generated internal state.

Flag anything that is ambiguous or accidentally tied to:

- Compose/Docker/Podman;
- Kubernetes/OpenShift;
- AWS/Azure/GCP;
- a specific managed service;
- a specific storage/network/identity product.

Ambiguous boundaries are release blockers only when they affect the frozen public contract or future portability.

## Developer-experience acceptance

- five-minute onboarding still works;
- normal configuration remains sparse;
- upgrades/migrations are low-friction;
- compatibility errors are actionable;
- implementation details stay out of normal output;
- human CLI, JSON and MCP agree on semantic truth;
- no speculative framework or provider abstraction was added only to satisfy future possibilities.

## Explicitly out of scope

- availability/HA/topology semantics;
- Kubernetes implementation;
- OpenShift implementation;
- AWS/Azure/GCP implementation;
- Operator/CRDs;
- OIDC/RBAC/JIT;
- air-gap/private-registry implementation;
- optional ecosystem expansion.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Full Compose reference lifecycle passes on the exact release head.
- [ ] Supported state migrations pass end to end.
- [ ] Public compatibility contracts are versioned/documented.
- [ ] Capability-provider compatibility is demonstrated.
- [ ] CLI/JSON/MCP expose the same underlying semantics.
- [ ] A generic coding agent completes the supported Compose lifecycle end to end without raw shell/Docker/Compose fallback.
- [ ] MCP covers the necessary semantic lifecycle without becoming a 1:1 CLI mirror.
- [ ] Portable application intent contains no runtime/cloud-vendor realization details.
- [ ] Architecture review confirms Kubernetes/OpenShift/AWS/Azure/GCP remain implementable without fundamental contract rewrite.
- [ ] Backup/restore, repair and destroy remain ownership-safe.
- [ ] Documentation matches current behavior and clearly marks future behavior.
- [ ] Validation is truthful and economical; unnecessary GitHub Actions are not used.
- [ ] Remaining blockers for the next phase are explicit and limited to genuine missing platform primitives.

Depends on: #175, #297, #298, #299
Parent roadmap: #155


## Delivery portability acceptance

Before v0.5 closes, prove by contract/fixture that the same portable application intent can be associated with different deployment delivery strategies without changing application semantics.

At minimum:

- direct delivery remains the Compose reference behavior;
- a delegated delivery fixture/stub can represent desired revision, synchronization state and reconciliation ownership without introducing GitOps-product fields into portable intent;
- conflicting reconciliation ownership fails closed.

This is a contract acceptance test, not yet a real Argo CD implementation.


## Pre-release gate

Before creating this release:

- [ ] All acceptance criteria in this issue are complete.
- [ ] Required local/repository tests pass.
- [ ] The full relevant CI matrix has passed at least once on the **exact release-candidate commit**.
- [ ] Docker and Podman acceptance pass where applicable.
- [ ] Security, isolation and secret-leak checks pass where applicable.
- [ ] The documentation audit defined by #364 passes.
- [ ] Human-facing documentation matches the shipped behavior.
- [ ] Reference and normative specs match every changed public contract.
- [ ] No unresolved release blocker remains.
- [ ] Version, changelog, release notes and release metadata are consistent.
- [ ] Final exact-head acceptance evidence is recorded before tagging/releasing.

Acceptance answers whether the feature/release scope is complete. This gate answers whether the exact commit is safe and documented well enough to release.

Do not weaken or skip a required check merely to complete the release. Checks that are genuinely not applicable should be recorded as such rather than silently omitted.


## Provider Catalog portability acceptance

The final v0.5 acceptance must prove the frozen Provider Catalog contract can resolve all three provider families without changing portable application intent.

Contract/fixture acceptance must cover:

```text
Provider Catalog
  -> RuntimeProvider
  -> CapabilityProvider
  -> DeliveryProvider

OCI artifact
  -> immutable digest identity

resolved selection
  -> deployment/provider state

instantiated provider
  -> Provider Runtime Registry / bindings where applicable
```

At minimum prove:

- the same catalog contract represents Runtime, Capability and Delivery Provider families while keeping their responsibilities separate;
- provider discovery metadata is not runtime instance/binding state;
- provider resolution can select an OCI artifact by immutable digest;
- a catalog entry with an unsupported Provider Protocol or service-contract version is rejected before mutation;
- Capability Provider substitution is allowed only when the required semantic subset is satisfied;
- Delivery Provider substitution does not change portable application intent;
- Runtime Provider substitution remains deployment/operator state;
- a provider artifact/version change is observable through status/plan/evidence where relevant.

This is contract/fixture acceptance. A hosted public marketplace, registry UI and broad third-party ecosystem remain outside v0.5.

### Provider Catalog acceptance

- [ ] Provider Catalog and Provider Runtime Registry boundaries are proven separately.
- [ ] Runtime, Capability and Delivery provider descriptors validate against the frozen catalog schema.
- [ ] OCI artifact reference/digest consistency is verified.
- [ ] Unsupported descriptor/protocol/contract combinations fail before mutation.
- [ ] Provider replacement preserves portable application intent when compatibility requirements are satisfied.


## Third-party runtime portability proof

Final v0.5 portability acceptance must prove the runtime boundary from #396 independently of Docker/Podman product details.

At minimum:

- a fake/reference conforming runtime provider can implement the frozen runtime boundary without changing portable application intent;
- the proof does not require product-specific branches in BaseHarbor Core;
- unsupported runtime semantics fail before mutation through provider-neutral capability/compatibility results;
- Docker and Podman remain reference implementations, not privileged Core paths;
- the proof documents which semantics come from adopted standards and which minimal semantics are BaseHarbor extensions.

No Kubernetes implementation is required for this proof.
